name: Letybo

lead: Letybo is a brand of letibotulinumtoxinA, a botulinum toxin type A that clinicians inject to soften the frown lines between the eyebrows. People use it for a smoother, less tense upper face, with the softening showing within days.

The toxin blocks acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction, relaxing the injected muscle so the lines above it ease. The FDA approved it for glabellar lines in February 2024, and the same toxin is sold in Korea as Botulax. Published work includes observational studies of upper-face treatment and a registered comparison with other toxins for forehead lines.

paras: A clinician injects the frown-line area in a short office visit, and people typically return for repeat sessions as the effect wears off over a few months. It is often used alongside other upper-face toxin treatments or skin care for a general anti-aging routine.

Reported effects include headache, eyelid and brow drooping and eyelid twitching. It is prescription-only, the effect is temporary, and botulinum toxins carry class warnings about spread of toxin effect beyond the injection site.

angle.text: Letybo softens the frown lines between the eyebrows, giving a smoother, more relaxed upper face within days of the injection. It works by relaxing the frown muscles so the overlying lines ease. It is one of several botulinum toxin brands, and glabellar lines are the use it was approved and trialled for.

lead: Letybo is a brand of letibotulinumtoxinA, a botulinum toxin type A injectable made by Hugel of South Korea and marketed in Europe with Croma Pharma [1]. It is used to relax the muscles that pull the brows together, smoothing the vertical frown lines between the eyebrows (glabellar lines) so the face looks less tense and often younger. In practice, clinicians also use it across the upper face, including forehead and crow's feet lines [2][3]. The US Food and Drug Administration approved it for glabellar lines in February 2024.

The same toxin is sold in Korea and other markets as Botulax [4]. Its US approval followed three BLESS phase 3 trials enrolling about 1,271 adults with moderate to severe glabellar lines at 31 sites in the US and EU, comparing a single treatment with placebo. Its most common side effects are headache, eyelid and brow drooping, and eyelid twitching.

Published research includes the pivotal trials and their pooled quality-of-life analysis, a 2026 meta-analysis of the randomised trials, expert consensus statements on upper-face technique, and real-world reports [5][6][7].
infobox: Hugel (Korea); Croma Pharma partner in Europe [1]

paras: Letybo is indicated in the US for temporary improvement of the appearance of moderate to severe glabellar lines. A 2024 consensus from seven aesthetic experts from South Korea and Australia gave recommendations for treating forehead horizontal lines, glabellar lines and lateral canthal lines with letibotulinumtoxinA, covering anatomy, patient selection and complication avoidance [2]. A separate 2023 consensus addressed its use in Asian patients, noting that many prefer natural-looking results and describing three goals: wrinkle softening, contour adjustment and face lifting [7].

A 2025 real-world report examined the toxin in routine upper-face practice, looking at the interplay of elevator and depressor muscles in the forehead and brow [3]. Two completed observational studies registered in 2025 and 2026 covered upper-face and periorbital treatment [8][9]. The Toxins narrative review of cosmetic botulinum toxin in the oral and maxillofacial area lists letibotulinumtoxinA among the FDA-approved products and describes uses such as masseter slimming and gummy smile correction for botulinum toxins as a class [10].
A 2026 randomised, double-blind trial in 20 women tested letibotulinumtoxinA for trapezius hypertrophy, an aesthetic concern about shoulder and neck contour [11].
Under the name Botulax, a randomised, double-blind, multi-centre phase 3 trial tested the toxin in post-stroke upper limb spasticity [4].

Botulinum toxin type A blocks release of acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction, weakening the injected muscle. Formulations of type A toxin differ mainly in the excipients that determine stability, aggregation and diffusion; a 2026 in silico modelling study compared six marketed products [12]. A 2026 review of Korean toxins describes 15 Korean manufacturers registering 19 toxin drugs in Korea, and names letibotulinumtoxinA (Hugel with Croma Pharma) and prabotulinumtoxinA (Daewoong with Evolus) as the two Korean products registered in both the USA and Europe [1].

Wikipedia reports that the most common effects of Letybo are headache, eyelid and brow drooping, and eyelid twitching. In the BLESS pooled meta-analysis of three randomised trials, the safety analysis showed no significant increase in serious, non-serious or overall treatment-emergent adverse events compared with placebo [5]. Botulinum toxins as a class carry labelling about spread of toxin effect from the injection site, which the FDA highlighted in 2008 and 2009 through a notice and boxed warnings. Cosmetic use of botulinum toxin has been associated with temporary facial weakness, bruising and, rarely, double vision.

Botulinum toxin entered cosmetic medicine in 2002 with Botox Cosmetic, and later entrants included Dysport, Xeomin, Jeuveau (made by Daewoong) in 2019 and Daxxify in 2022. Korea's toxin industry grew quickly as aesthetic demand surged, with Neuronox registered in 2006 as the first Korean product [1]. Letybo's approval in the US in February 2024 added a further Korean-made toxin to the American market [1].

In looksmaxxing discussion, newer and imported toxin brands are talked about as alternatives to the best-known brands. Expert consensus papers on the product emphasise individualised treatment plans and natural-looking results [2][7].

The BLESS I, II and III trials randomised adults aged 18 to 75 with moderate to severe glabellar lines to a single treatment or placebo. A 2026 meta-analysis of three randomised trials with 1,272 patients found letibotulinumtoxinA-wlbg significantly more effective than placebo on the composite responder rate at week 4, with effects sustained at weeks 12 and 16 and improvements in investigator-assessed, subject-assessed and psychological outcomes [5].

A pooled analysis of the BLESS trials found that 85.5 percent of treated subjects had moderate to severe psychological impact from their lines at baseline, and treated subjects improved significantly more than placebo on all measures, including a mean change of -33.84 points on the glabellar line quality-of-life scale versus -1.37 with placebo, along with FACE-Q appraisal and age-appraisal outcomes [6].

A registered phase 4 study compared letibotulinum toxin A with other toxin products for forehead wrinkles, measuring safety, efficacy and diffusion in 20 adults. The 2025 clinical-practice report and the two completed non-interventional studies are small and observational [8][9][3].
